meta.title: Who really said "Will you have sugar and cream in your nose?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not J. P. Morgan's line. The tea-party joke appears anonymously in Mary Roberts Rinehart's 1928 Saturday Evening Post piece; Anne Morrow Lindbergh denied it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Will you have sugar and cream in your nose?'?
meta.ogDescription: Morgan never said it, and it probably never happened. The earliest printing, from January 1928, names nobody; the child in the story called the tale untrue.

answer.label: Not J. P. Morgan — a joke line, earliest printed by Mary Roberts Rinehart
answer.authorDates: 1876–1958 · American novelist · earliest documented printing, 14 Jan 1928
answer.sourceLine: Morgan never said this: in every version of the story the line is the flustered hostess’s blunder, and Morgan is the guest with the famously disfigured nose. The earliest printing Quote Investigator can find is Mary Roberts Rinehart’s humour piece “Just a Touch of Celebrity” in The Saturday Evening Post of 14 January 1928, where nobody is named — the financier is only “Mr. Blank.” Morgan’s name was grafted on by 1936, and Anne Morrow Lindbergh, cast as the child in the tale, later said it had “not a grain of truth in it.”

source.excerpt: [A great financier with a very large and bulbous nose is coming to Sunday luncheon. The small boy, Johnnie, is warned neither to stare at the nose nor to mention it. He does neither; when the coffee comes on he is excused, and his relieved mother turns to the guest:] “Mr. Blank, will you have sugar and cream in your nose?”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ states that the earliest match for the tale it located is Mary Roberts Rinehart’s piece in The Saturday Evening Post of 14 January 1928, where the guest is “Mr. Blank” and the punchline is “will you have sugar and cream in your nose?”

The joke was still anonymous in 1933, when a Brooklyn Daily Eagle version by Art Arthur called the guest “Mr. Van Blank”; O. O. McIntyre’s syndicated column of 10 February 1936 is the version that names Morgan, the Morrows and their daughter, per QI’s citations ↗.
Morgan died on 31 March 1913 — Wikipedia ↗ — fifteen years before the first printing of the joke and twenty-three before his name was attached to it.

Biographer Jean Strouse tracked the story down and printed the refutation: her New Yorker essay of 29 March 1999 ↗ reports that Dwight Morrow only joined the bank after Morgan’s death and that Anne Morrow Lindbergh confirmed the tale has “not a grain of truth in it,” while conceding it is too funny to die.
source.excerptNote: The setup is summarised; the punchline is the wording as transcribed by Quote Investigator from the January 1928 Saturday Evening Post. Note the guest is “Mr. Blank” — the version that supplies the famous wording is the version that names no one.

source.rightsNote: The wording’s earliest documented home is a periodical from January 1928 — The Saturday Evening Post of 14 January that year, which entered the United States public domain on 1 January 2024, when the 95-year copyright term for 1928 publications expired. The anecdote itself is anonymous folklore with no identifiable owner. Two honest caveats: the 1928 text is cited here from Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗ rather than from our own inspection of the issue, and the modern retellings quoted on this page (Jean Strouse’s 1999 essay in particular) remain in copyright to their authors and publishers.

author.name: Mary Roberts Rinehart
author.heading: Who actually put this line in print
author.metaLine: 1876–1958 · American mystery novelist & Saturday Evening Post regular
author.bio: Mary Roberts Rinehart was one of the best-selling American writers of the early twentieth century — a mystery novelist whose breakthrough, The Circular Staircase (1908), helped invent the “had I but known” suspense style, and a prolific contributor to The Saturday Evening Post whose books had sold well over ten million copies by her death. Her January 1928 Post essay on the perils of celebrity contains the earliest printing of this joke that quote researchers have located, told about an unnamed financier and an unnamed hostess. That makes her the first documented teller, not necessarily the inventor: the comic situation — a child who might remark on a guest’s nose — was already in print decades earlier, in the 1901 recitation book The New Century Speaker, though there the child speaks and there is no coached silence and no adult’s slip.

misattribution.heading: Who gets credited, and why it fails
misattribution.intro: This is a quote that gets pinned on J. P. Morgan even though he is the person it is aimed at. Three separate errors are usually stacked on top of each other.

items.why: Morgan is the guest, not the speaker. In every recorded version the line is the hostess’s slip after she has spent the afternoon dreading that her child would mention his nose — Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the joke works only that way ↗. Nothing resembling the line appears among his own documented remarks on Wikiquote ↗.

items.who: Elizabeth Cutter Morrow, with Anne Morrow Lindbergh as the child
items.why: Named tellings put Morgan in the Morrows’ drawing room from 1936 onward, but Jean Strouse, who worked for years in the Morgan archives, reports that Dwight Morrow did not join the bank until after Pierpont Morgan died, and that Anne Morrow Lindbergh confirmed to her that the tale has “not a grain of truth in it” ↗. Wikipedia’s article on Morrow dates his partnership to 1913 ↗ — the year Morgan died, that March — so even the most generous reading leaves almost no window for the visit.

“Sugar and cream in your nose” belongs to the 1928 version in which nobody is identified. The Morgan-named tellings say something else: “cream or lemon in your nose” in O. O. McIntyre’s column of 10 February 1936, and “one lump or two” in later retellings, as QI’s citation list sets out ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a floating joke, not a quotation: the earliest printing researchers have found ↗ names no one, Morgan’s name arrived twenty-three years after his death in 1913, and the woman supposedly in the room said it never happened.

context.heading: Why this joke stuck to Morgan
lead: J. Pierpont Morgan had rhinophyma, a disfiguring consequence of rosacea that swelled and reddened his nose; Wikipedia notes the deformity and how self-conscious he was about being photographed ↗, and popular accounts compared the nose to a purple cauliflower. He was also the most powerful banker in the world. A joke that needs a famous man with an unmentionable face had an obvious magnet, and it found him.

Jean Strouse, who spent years in the Morgan archives writing his biography, described the story as ubiquitous — one of two anecdotes strangers volunteered to her at dinner parties, the other being the quip about what a yacht costs. The tea party she could disprove from the record: Dwight Morrow was not yet at the bank. The yacht line she doubted on different grounds, calling it implausible for a man she describes as “singularly inarticulate, unreflective… not likely to come up with a maxim worthy of Oscar Wilde.” Her New Yorker essay is where the denial was finally put in print.
context.detailsSummary: The older version of the joke, and the wording drift
detailsBody: The setup predates Morgan’s fame as a punchline target. Quote Investigator points to a 1901 recitation book, The New Century Speaker, in which a child asks a visitor about the lump on his nose — the same comic situation without the luncheon table or the adult’s slip. See QI’s chronology ↗.

The familiar wording is itself a fossil of the anonymous version. “Sugar and cream in your nose” is Rinehart’s 1928 phrasing about “Mr. Blank”; the tellings that actually name Morgan use different words — “cream or lemon in your nose” in O. O. McIntyre’s 1936 column, and “one lump or two in your nose” in the version Strouse recounts. Anyone quoting “sugar and cream” and crediting Morgan is combining a wording from the version that names nobody with a cast list added years later.
context.pull: “Not a grain of truth in it” — Anne Morrow Lindbergh, the child in the story
